questions.question: What is the range of a linear map $A:V\to W$?
options: The set of vectors in $V$ not used by $A$.
The set of inputs sent to zero.
The set of outputs $Av$ obtained from vectors $v\in V$.

questions.question: Where does the range live?
What does the range measure informally?
options: The list of all scalars in the field.
The number of equations defining the map.
The part of the domain sent to zero.
The part of the codomain actually reached by the map.

questions.question: What kind of subset is the range of a linear map?
options: A subspace of the domain only.
A set of scalars, not vectors.

questions.question: When is a linear map surjective?
options: When its kernel is the whole domain.
When its range equals its codomain.
When it sends every input to zero.

questions.question: For $A(x,y)=(x,0)$ on $\mathbb R^2$, what is the range?
What is the range of the zero map $Z:V\to W$?
For $A(t)=(t,2t)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R^2$, which vector lies in the range?
What is the range of the identity map $I:V\to V$?
For $A(x,y)=(x+y,0)$, which output can occur?
How is range different from codomain?
options: The codomain consists only of inputs.
The range is the codomain vectors that are actually hit
The range is always larger than the codomain
There is no difference for any function.

questions.question: Why is the range a subspace for linear maps?
options: Linear combinations of reached outputs are also reached
The range is defined by removing the zero vector
Only the zero map has a range.
Every subset of the codomain is a subspace.

questions.question: What does failure of surjectivity mean in terms of range?
options: Some codomain vectors are not in the range.
The range contains vectors outside the codomain.

questions.question: For $A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ given by $A(x,y)=x-y$, what is the range?
For $A(x,y,z)=(x,y)$ from $\mathbb R^3$ to $\mathbb R^2$, is $A$ surjective?
options: Yes, every $(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2$ is reached by $(a,b,0)$.
No, because the domain has more coordinates.
Yes, but only the zero vector is reached.

questions.question: For $A(t)=(t,t,t)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R^3$, what is the range?
Can the range equal the codomain even when the kernel is not $\{0\}$?
options: Yes, for maps from a larger domain onto a smaller codomain
No, a nontrivial kernel makes the range empty
Yes, but only for nonlinear maps.

questions.question: Why is saying “$w\in\operatorname{range}A$” an existence statement?
options: It means there exists some $v\in V$ with $Av=w$.
It means $w$ lies in the kernel.

questions.question: For $A(x,y)=(x+y,x+y)$, which vector is not in the range?
If $\operatorname{range}A=\operatorname{span}((1,2))$, which codomain vector is reached?
